title: 3-Read Friday #52: Analogies, To-Do Lists, and the Science of Reading
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 52 of Craig Barton's weekly roundup features three picks with a strong cognitive-science and personal thread running through his commentary. He highlights Blake Harvard's use of musical and sporting analogies to sell students on retrieval practice over rereading, a device Barton frames as solving the classic motivation problem around effortful study. He then recommends Ian Frost's reframing of the to-do list as a 'done list', a leadership-productivity idea he simply says he likes. The third pick is Doug Lemov's overview of the science of reading 'post-phonics', which Barton connects to a personal thread -- watching his son Isaac learn phonics -- as well as a professional interest in comparing reading development to maths development. The issue closes with the usual sign-off pointing to his newsletter archive.
points: Barton values Harvard's analogy device specifically because it solves a motivational problem with retrieval practice, not just an explanatory one -- students avoid effortful methods because they feel unpleasant, and analogies to sport/music reframe that discomfort as expected.
He picks Frost's 'done list' reframing without much elaboration, signalling it as a lightweight but appealing productivity idea for school leaders rather than a research-backed practice.

He explicitly draws a parallel between reading development and maths development as two subject-specific applications of the same underlying learning-science questions, a recurring theme in his curation.
The personal framing (his son learning phonics) shows how Barton uses his own parenting experience as a lens for evaluating professional reading research, not just abstract interest.
quotes: Showing students the purpose of what they are doing is a good way to get them on board so they put in the required effort to learn.
However, this can be challenging for an abstract concept such as retrieval.
I have a personal interest in reading development at the moment as I watch my eldest son, Isaac, get to grips with phonics.
I also have a professional interest as I look for similarities and differences between maths development and reading development.
This blog from Doug provides a great overview of the science of reading research.
